label: explain2-bm-making
one_line: We want to make a plastic strip that curls on its own when damp, like a pine cone scale. First we must measure how much the plastic swells.
what: Our goal is a window shade that moves by itself when the air gets damp, with no motor. Picture a pine cone. Each scale is two layers stuck together. When one layer swells more than the other, the scale bends. We want to copy that with 3D-printed plastic. We would stick one layer that swells when wet onto one layer that hardly swells. Wet the strip and it curls, like a leaf curling as it dries. A written rule, worked out by the engineer Stephen Timoshenko in 1925, says how far such a strip can bend. It was first written for thermostat strips made of two metals that bend when heated. The rule depends on how much the wet layer grows and how thick the strip is. We have planned five things to print. The first is a small strip, about as long as a paper clip (30 by 3 by 1 millimetres). The last is a small shade module, a single slat about as long as your hand (120 millimetres). Before any of that, we must soak small test strips and measure how much each plastic swells. Nobody has published that number for these plastics.
why: Buildings use motors and sensors to open and close shades. A shade that moves with the damp in the air would need no power. A rule that predicts the bend lets a designer plan such a part before printing it. First we must learn whether the rule works for cheap, common printer plastics. Nobody has measured how much these plastics swell in damp air. Every prediction rests on one data sheet from the maker. We do not know yet if the idea works. The first test is small. It costs about a thousand dollars in materials, if the lab borrows the big machines. That is roughly the price of a decent laptop. We soak the strips in liquid water, not damp air, for a practical reason. Water gives the biggest swelling, so it is the easiest first test. Damp air will swell the plastic less. If it swelled only one tenth as much, our louver (slat) would turn about 6 degrees instead of about 58. So the water test only shows whether the idea can work at all. Damp air must be tested next.

steps.text: Print flat test strips from several Formlabs plastics. The Form 4 printer holds one plastic at a time, so each plastic is a separate print.
steps.picture: Like baking one flavour of cookie per tray.

steps.text: Rinse the strips in rubbing alcohol (isopropanol, a cleaning liquid). Dry them, then bake them under light. Weigh them again and again until the weight stops dropping. That means no more liquid is left inside.
steps.picture: Like weighing laundry on the line until it stops getting lighter.

steps.text: Measure each strip's length and thickness before it gets wet. Use a fixed camera with a ruler in the picture.
steps.picture: Like marking a child's height on a door frame, always from the same spot.

steps.text: Soak the strips in water and weigh them at set times. Use a fine scale and wipe each strip the same way every time. A thin film of water on the surface can weigh as much as the water inside.
steps.picture: Like weighing a sponge: squeeze it the same way each time.

steps.text: Measure the length again after soaking. On a 40 millimetre strip, the length changes by about 2 parts in 1,000. That is about 80 micrometres, roughly the width of one human hair.
steps.picture: A strip as long as a pencil stub that grows by one hair's width.

steps.text: Glue or print a swelling layer onto a layer that hardly swells. Note the thickness of each.
steps.picture: Like pressing a damp paper towel onto a dry plastic ruler.

steps.text: Wet the two-layer strip and photograph its curl from the side. Fit a circle to the curve. The size of that circle tells us how tight the bend is.
steps.picture: Like tracing a round plate to find its size.

steps.text: Compare the measured bend with the bend the written rule predicts from the swelling numbers.
steps.picture: Like checking a recipe's promised cooking time against your oven.

wrong_if: Our bet, written before we look: a strip with measured layer swelling and thickness will curl to within a fifth of the rule's prediction. For the first strip, the prediction is a curl with a radius of about 41 millimetres. A 41 millimetre radius is a circle a little wider than a bottle cap's diameter, times about two. We ran many computer trials with our best guesses for the unknown inputs. Nine out of ten trials landed between 28 and 83 millimetres. We are wrong if the real curl is far outside that range. We are also wrong if the plastic swells too little to see.
could_go_wrong: The swelling numbers come from one data sheet. It does not say how thick the tested slab was.
The plastics may swell much less in damp air than in liquid water. Then the strips may barely bend. Our notes say we have no data on damp air at all.
The two layers may not stick to each other well. Nobody has measured that bond.
Alcohol left inside a strip after rinsing could be mistaken for swelling in water.
The signal is tiny, about 80 micrometres (one hair's width) on a 40 millimetre strip. A cheap ruler or caliper cannot measure it.

The rule assumes the layers are stuck together perfectly and that the bends are small. The real strip may break both assumptions. A bend that is too tight, or a join that slips, would make the rule fail.
Thick layers soak slowly. Doubling the length makes the wait four times longer. A shade one metre wide could need about 184 days (our estimate, from 54 to 660) to finish bending.
We estimated, not measured, how stiff the plastic is when wet. A wrong guess may shift the predicted bend.

questions.q: How do you know the bend rule is right?
questions.a: We re-ran the project's check script and an independent solver. They agree to about one part in a billion. That shows the maths is consistent. It does not show that real plastic obeys the rule.

questions.q: How do you know these plastics swell at all?
questions.a: One data sheet for Flexible 80A V2 says it gains 8 percent in mass and 3 percent in volume in one day in water. Other Formlabs plastics gain under 1 percent in their cube test. One older soft one gains 2.3 percent.

questions.q: Why test in liquid water if the shade will sit in damp air?
questions.a: Water is the strongest case, so it is the easiest first test. If the strip cannot bend in water, it will not bend in air. Damp air will swell the plastic less. We have no measurement of how much less. If it swelled one tenth as much, the slat would turn about 6 degrees instead of about 58. Damp air is the next test, not this one.

questions.q: What would the shade look like?
questions.a: Our biggest planned part is one slat, 120 millimetres long, about the length of your hand. Wet in water, we predict it turns about 58 degrees (likely range 30 to 85). That is roughly like tilting a door a bit more than halfway open. A real shade would be many such slats. We have not designed one, and we have not built anything yet. Large slats are a problem. A long, soft slat held sideways also sags under its own weight more than it curls.

questions.q: What are the five things you plan to print?
questions.a: One: a small strip, 30 by 3 by 1 millimetres. Two: a row of ten fingers of different widths, to test how the bend changes with width. Three: tiles of growing width, up to 60 millimetres, to see when a strip becomes a plate that the rule does not cover. Four: a tree that splits twice, with thick and thin branches, to see if all turn by the same angle. Five: the 120 millimetre slat. The first three look possible with stock plastics in under a week. Fourth is riskier because its thinnest branch is 0.2 millimetres thick. The fifth can be tested in water only.

questions.q: Has anyone built a damp-air bending part from printed resin before?
questions.a: Partly. A 2024 paper printed a polyurethane ink that folds in under one second in humid air. Polyurethane is a stretchy plastic. That ink is not a Formlabs plastic, and its bend was not compared with the rule. We found no part checked against a law whose maths a proof assistant has verified. A proof assistant is software that checks maths step by step. That is only what our search found. It does not prove no such part exists.

questions.q: Why is the swelling so hard to measure?
questions.a: The change is tiny and surface water confuses scales. It needs a fine scale, a fixed camera and a fixed routine.

questions.q: Would alcohol work better than water?
questions.a: Alcohol makes the soft plastic gain about 39 percent in a day. A hard plastic gains under 0.1 percent. That is far stronger. But the strips would stretch too much for the simple rule.

questions.q: Can I repeat this at home?
questions.a: Partly. A phone and a kitchen scale can show whether a strip curls. They cannot give numbers good enough to test the rule. Proper kit costs one to two thousand dollars. Buying every core item new would cost $9,017 to $11,524. We think most of that can be borrowed, which leaves $920 to $1,231 to buy. Some printer-setting costs are separate. Formlabs sells a mode for using other makers' resin (Open Material Mode) for $875 per printer.

A 0.4 millimetre layer would settle in hours to about a day. The 120 millimetre slat would take about 2.7 days in water, and likely between under 1 day and 10 days. Both estimates assume a slab thickness the data sheet never states. They are our estimates, not measurements.
We have not printed or soaked any strip. We have not measured swelling in damp air, bond strength, or wet stiffness. Several prices came from search snippets only.

glossary.plain: A liquid plastic that hardens when light shines on it.
A machine that builds an object one thin layer at a time.
A company that makes resin 3D printers and the resins for them.
The Formlabs printer model we plan to use.
A Formlabs setting that lets the printer use resins from other makers. It costs $875 per Form 4.
A soft, rubber-like Formlabs resin that swells the most in water.
Softer rubber-like Formlabs resins, used here as the layer that hardly swells.
A very soft Formlabs resin made from silicone.
Hard Formlabs resins that swell very little.
A common plastic family that hardens under light. Many printer resins are of this kind.
A strip made of two stuck-together layers that react differently, so it bends.
A material that changes shape when the dampness of the air changes. A pine cone scale is one.
Stephen Timoshenko, an engineer who in 1925 wrote the rule for how a two-layer strip bends.
To grow in size by soaking up liquid.
How much water vapour is in the air.
Air holding a lot of water vapour.
Water as a gas in the air.
Water with its dissolved minerals removed, so it is very pure.
The slow spreading of water into a material, like tea colouring a sugar cube.
How tightly a strip curves. A small radius means a tight curl.
The distance from the centre of a circle to its edge, here used to describe a curl.
The 1925 formula by Timoshenko that predicts how far a two-layer strip bends.
A script that tests the rule's top value. The value tops out at 1.5 times a basic bend, and the script confirms nothing goes higher.
One thousandth of a metre, about the thickness of a credit card.
One thousandth of a millimetre. A human hair is about 70 of them wide.
How much matter something holds, which is what a scale reads.
How much space something takes up.
A maker's page of test results for a product.
Parts per hundred. 8 percent means 8 parts more for each 100.
The middle range of many trial results. We cut off the lowest 5 in 100 and the highest 5 in 100, so 9 in 10 fall inside.
The time for a curl to reach 90 and 99 percent of its final bend. Our notes do not state the unit of the printed numbers.
A rubbing alcohol used to rinse printed parts.
A hand tool that measures length to about a fortieth of a millimetre.
A device that weighs things. A fine one reads to a ten-thousandth of a gram.
A camera that never moves, so before and after photos match.
How hard a material pushes back when you bend or stretch it. A plastic can be stiffer dry than wet.
How well two layers stick to each other.
Software that checks a mathematical argument step by step.
A slanted slat in a window shade.
A soft, water-filled plastic that swells a lot.
A stretchy printable plastic liquid used in the 2024 paper.
Dry a sample until repeat weighings no longer drop.
One run of the printer with one resin in it.
A list of every part to buy, with its price.

check_yourself.what: Open the Flexible 80A V2 data sheet, page 6, and find the Deionized Water row (water with minerals removed).
check_yourself.expect: 1 day: +8 percent mass, +3 percent volume. 1 week: +9 percent mass, +7 percent volume.

check_yourself.what: Re-run the project's bend-limit check. It only reads files.
check_yourself.expect: Last line: VERDICT: the ceiling holds in every check; grid maximum 1.499998 at m^2 n = 0.99996. In plain words: the limit held every time, and the highest value reached was just under 1.5. You can ignore the last number; it names the layer mix where that peak happened.

check_yourself.what: Recompute the instrument needs for the strips.
check_yourself.expect: Flexible 80A V2 strip 174.4 mg; 0.1 mg balance relative error 0.3 % at 8 % uptake; 80 um and 4.0 um length targets. In plain words: a strip weighs about 174 milligrams. A scale that reads to 0.1 milligram is off by only 0.3 percent when the strip gains 8 percent. The length changes to catch are 80 and 4 micrometres.

('ALL', 'core') $ 9016.50 - $ 11524.24 ; MUST_BUY core $919.98 - $1231.20. In plain words: all core items bought new cost about $9,017 to $11,524. The part we must buy, if we borrow the rest, is $920 to $1,231.

check_yourself.what: Re-run all bend models and the seeded random trials (random trials that give the same answer each run).
check_yourself.expect: Object 1 pair A R_final median 41.0 mm, 5th to 95th 27.6 to 83.3 mm; curvature t90 0.719 and t99 1.653. In plain words: the middle result for the first strip is a 41 millimetre radius, and 9 in 10 trials fall between 28 and 83. The t numbers are the times to reach 90 and 99 percent of the final bend.

left_out: Claim that no design checked by a proof assistant exists anywhere: left out as fact, because it is a search absence the verifier did not test. Kept only as a hedged search result.
Claim that humidity actuators are slow and weak compared with heat-driven ones: left out as fact, only partly supported and a judgement. The 2024 film folds in under 1 second.

Claim that all Form 4 resins are acrylates (a common light-hardening plastic family) and that no bond data exists: left out. Only 14 safety sheets were checked, so this is a gap in what we searched, not a finding.
Claim that Flexible 80A V2 is the only resin that swells much: left out, because the older Elastic 50A V1 gains 2.3 percent in water.
Claim that no measurement of humid-air swelling exists at all: left out as fact, since sources cannot prove a negative. We only say we found none.

Claim that the Open Material Mode price of 3748.50 dollars was wrong: left out, because the earlier file was not read. Only the 875 dollar per-printer price is confirmed. It is now mentioned in the home-repeat answer, with that one price only.
Claim that the best pairs reach 99 percent of the bend limit and stiff pairs lose 41 to 89 percent: left out, because it rests on guessed stiffness values.
Exact diffusion speed and settling times: used only as hedged ranges, because they assume a 2 mm slab the data sheet never states.
